claims.text: The initial near-equiatomic PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution and are uniformly dispersed on an inert oxide support.
Annealing PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles in H2 at 773 K for 1–2 hours induces a thin Pt/Pd-enriched surface layer.
Rapid cooling after reducing annealing kinetically locks in Pt/Pd surface segregation.
The Pt/Pd-enriched surface layer acts as a passivating shell.
The Pt/Pd-enriched shell retards atomic diffusion in the multi-element core.
The Pt/Pd-enriched shell suppresses nanoparticle coalescence and sintering.
The Pt/Pd-enriched shell suppresses phase and compositional segregation in the multi-element core.
Pt and Pd have lower diffusion barriers than the other relevant components of the nanoparticles.
Differences in oxidation potential help drive Pt and Pd toward the nanoparticle surface during reducing annealing.
Reducing annealing causes Pt and Pd to migrate preferentially to the surface of PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will retain a single-phase, homogeneous multi-element structure better than untreated nanoparticles after high-temperature cycling.
Annealed nanoparticles will coarsen less than untreated nanoparticles during high-temperature cycling.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional segregation than untreated nanoparticles during high-temperature cycling.
Improved structural retention will produce better retention of catalytic or thermoelectric properties.
Untreated PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles have a greater propensity for sintering and elemental segregation during high-temperature cycling.
The proposed stabilization mechanism is effective primarily under reducing conditions and optimized annealing parameters.
Excessive annealing time or temperature can cause over-segregation and compromise the integrity of the multi-element core.
The stabilization benefit diminishes under non-reducing atmospheres.
The optimal annealing conditions and resulting shell stability vary with nanoparticle size and support material.
